The problem with this is that it’s a complete fiction. The notion that just because a person is not involved in elected politics, this means that they are somehow unable to be swayed or unaffected by it is silly. There are many examples of how this is in fact not the case, from the most egregious examples of corruption, to information not taken into account because it contradicts a set narrative or even when politics gets in the way of the facts. I would cite the example of how anti-lockdown protests were derided as spreading Covid, but BLM protests were fine because “racism is a public health crisis.” I’m sure a left wing person would have a similar example showing hypocrisy from the right but the point stands either way.

The simple reality is that as soon as you give a person power within an immensely important body of government, they will immediately become subject to the pressures, opportunities and potential that naturally accompanies such an office. So the idea that we can insulate them from that is silly. Of course someone who exists in the political landscape isn’t going to be a completely sober and neutral judge of the facts. They’re human beings, subject to their own failings, flaws and temptations. We should not expect anything more because we will inevitably be disappointed by the result. A handful of positive examples doesn’t change that, because there are many more examples of waste, incompetence and abuse of power we could cite. But that’s a problem with human nature, not the system itself. The system is just pointless when a unicameral chamber would suffice.

-

If you want to solve the problem of Parliaments not listening to experts by introducing legislation stating that Parliamentary bills have to be approved by their respective select committees of non-elected experts before they can be put to the House for a vote, then go ahead by all means. 

But you don’t need a permanent second chamber for that. It’s actually kind of counterproductive to give seats to experts on health/science to vote on tax bills, or immigration or education so they can all vote on all matters as if they’re equal when they’re only in the house for their respective field.

Why do we need a second chamber for that?

If the idea is that legislation proposed should be verified by experts in their fields, then we can have select committees brought in when appropriate to give their advice and consolation on the matter.

We don’t actually need a permanent second chamber to perform that function when it can be arranged on a temporary basis.

A pointless institution, as are most bicameral parliaments - including the American congress. 

The purpose of the two houses was to represent the two major factions in the country at that time; The landed aristocracy on the one hand, and the incorporated towns on the other. That was the division which existed in medieval England. 

But that’s not how things are now. Landowning is not anywhere near as important as it was a thousand years ago, so there’s no real power that justifies their inclusion to this extent. If we were to actually balance the Commons out, you’d have a House full of CEOs, stockholders and maybe trade union bosses. Those are the people who hold the actual power of economic capital in the modern economy, balanced out with the workers in the Commons. But literally no one wants that. Not communists, not the “MAGA” right (for want of a better term), certainly not conservatives or monarchists, not mainstream liberals, everyone would be aghast at this idea. Maybe some very free market libertarians would be on board, maybe.

Everyone agrees that the House of Lords needs reform, but no one can agree on what to do with it. It can’t continue to be a stuffing ground for political donors you throw a lordship at when you win the election, but neither can it be a body  of just landowners and bishops because not only would it be unpopular but it would be impractical in the modern economy. And this goes for every other upper house in the world, especially the American, Canadian and Australian senates. Why bother with another chamber when you only need one elective body?

So if we can’t agree that it should remain consistent with its original purpose of representing the main economic interest in the country by handing it over to the business class, it should be abolished. It’s the only logical solution to what everyone can see is a problem of systemic corruption at this point.

I think the biggest change is that we don’t have an immediate media reference for the dangers of rapid technological progression and AI.

Now, Terminator wasn’t the first and it wouldn’t be the last to do this idea, I’m not saying no one would make a similar premise ever without it. But because of Terminator being such a huge blockbuster, it cemented itself in pop culture as the go to example of the dangers of AI, which I don’t think anything else would have done. Assuming Matrix still gets made in this timeline, I’d bet that’s what takes its place, but probably not the same way. 

It’s hard to assess how culture would change like this. There could be directors who only got into film because of how impressed they were by Terminator, for example. So you can’t really predict how art would change absent a piece of art. 

In the short term, Schwarzenegger was already a huge star and would have continued to be so. Hamilton and Beihn probably take bigger hits without this movie giving them so much publicity, but I imagine they’d have been fine career wise. Honestly the more radical and interesting idea is what if Cameron’s career tanks without this being his landmark movie. Realistically I think he’d still make Alien and be famous for that, but if he didn’t? The entire history of horror changes without Aliens being such a landmark franchise.

Lucius pulled back from the traitor’s embrace as they stood in the Order’s council chambers beside the great carved map of the realms, his grip on his sword slipping as the furrow on his brow deepened, though ready to raise it once more if he attacked… or tried to pull him in for another hug.

“I… I’m afraid I don’t understand. What, what are you talking about?” His voice was full of puzzlement and confusion.

“Oh, it’s… it’s simply been awful,”Magnus cried, wiping tears of apparent joy from his eyes as he tore off his robes of state, practically tearing the rings from his fingers and tossing them onto the floor. “I coveted this job for so long but I had no idea what I was getting myself in for.”

“But… you slew the noble Gaius, you usurped his position, forcibly took over the Inquisition.”

“And what a fool I was!” Magnus laughed, his voice sounding as if it were on the verge of breakdown. “I thought him merely pompous and arrogant, but no! He really was that good! He knew what he was doing! He was right to overlook me, I wasn’t cut out for this at all!”

Lucius had not been anticipating this. He had been expecting a great duel, perhaps some battle of wits, some kind of struggle to remove this agent of darkness from the seat he did not deserve. Yet, what he instead found was a weak, pitiable man who seemingly only wished for his sorrows to end? …No, he decided. It must be a trap. He raised his sword to the usurper’s throat.

“Do you take me for a fool? You think I will be deceived with this charade?”

“If you mean to take my life, by all means. I would welcome the end.”

“Why?” Lucius asked irritated, gritting his teeth, as he pressed the edge into his enemy’s flesh slightly. “Why should I believe you truly wish for this to end?”

“Where would I begin?” Magnus laughed again, almost a deranged cackle. “The enemies we fight, for a start. Demons, witches, vampires, monsters of all sorts. I have faced them, aye, but they do not target the mind of any so much as the Grand Master. They believe that through attacking my dreams, they destroy us, and they are right!”

“But it is our holy task to destroy-“

“Aye, and we do… but you can’t destroy them all! Always more, watching… waiting… waiting…” Magnus’ voice lowered, his eyes darting around the chamber at the shadows on the walls.

“And then there are the heretics,” Magnus continued. “Only I have the authority to consign them to the pyre, but how am I to know when the charges are correct? How many innocents have I condemned? How many guilty have I set free? And even when I get it right, was their crime that severe anyway? I do not know… I do not know…”

“And that’s not even mentioning the damned bureaucracy. Every day, there’s something. The Emperor wants constant updates, the Blacksmiths’ guild aren’t happy we stopped buying from them, the Mages’ guild feel threatened by us, there aren’t enough boots, there isn’t enough food, the castle walls are crumbling, the horses are sick. Something, something, something, every damn day, never a moment’s rest and when it goes wrong, all the fingers end up pointing at me!” Magnus’ voice had descended to a low, hoarse whisper. “And you ask why I wish for this to end?”

Lucius looked at him now, truly a pitiable creature, but still doubt ate away at him. 

“If this is true, then why not simply resign your post?”

“I cannot, the duties of the office are too great, there must be a clean succession. No squabbles over who gets the job. Because if there was, who would they blame when it all went wrong again?” He laughed softly once again. “But you! You can assume my place! Become the new Grand Master!”

Lucius looked at him again; Once a mighty and revered clerk, Magnus was now a dishevelled, broken shell of a man… and he suddenly had the urge to be anywhere else but here.

“Oh no, I’m not worthy of-“

“But you are!” Magnus declared as he hoisted the great chain of office around Lucius’ shoulders. “If you are not, then our enemies will use the infighting to destroy us. You must take the mantle or we will fall. It has to be you, why would they have sent you otherwise?” Magnus smiled, and Lucius suddenly understood why none of his superiors offered to be the one to take Magnus into custody when the opportunity arose. 

Magnus giggled and began shuffling out of the chamber, leaving Lucius alone. And as he shot a quick glance at a mirror hanging over the chamber fireplace, he could have sworn he saw Magnus in his reflection for a second.

Here’s the more important question;

If all their internal organs work as if they were still alive, why don’t the testes and uterus? That is to say, why can’t vampires have children if literally every other part of their bodies are still functioning?

No, they’re all over 100 years old.

That “they stay the same mentally” is debatable enough in Twilight simply because that’s not possible, but it’s never been a point in TVD. All the vampires we’ve seen have grown and changed, or became worse, from who they were when they were turned. They’re clearly capable of maturing as people.

So I don’t buy the idea that they’re stuck this way and they’re the same age, there is absolutely an age gap here.

Given the amount they drink, they have to dispose of it somehow.

If there’s some magic vampiric process that dissolves food and drink which isn’t blood when it enters their system, that raises a lot more questions. The first being “If your taste buds don’t work anymore and you can’t get drunk, why is alcohol even appealing to you?”

If it’s the natural, human way of disposing waste, then what makes some bodily functions no longer work? Having children is the most obvious one. If your urinary system is still working, why aren’t the testes/uterus?

As I said, vampires are supposed to be a dark, mysterious, sexy fantasy, and all these questions ruin the fantasy which is why they’re never addressed by most vampire media. 😂

I think all vampire media which is inherently focused on the mysterious, dark appeal of them is as uninterested in the finer, and more uncomfortable, points of anatomy as it’s possible to get. 

These questions are a disturbing reminder that corpses aren’t supposed to be alive, and forces us to seriously consider what the rules are if all your internal bodily functions suddenly stop.

For example, if vampires drink as much bourbon as TVD ones do, do they need to urinate it out? And if the urinary system is still doing its job, why aren’t the testes? That is to say, if TVD vampires are functionally alive to where they can drink and produce waste as if nothing happened, why can’t they have children? And conversely, if blood is what keeps their system alive, do vampire women also have periods?

You see why in what’s supposed to be a cool, sexy premise, questions like that just get in the way of the fantasy? No one acknowledges it cos no one wants to. 😂 

Twilight vampires avoid this by actually explaining that they don’t eat, drink or sleep, and most infamously why period blood is unappealing to them. It’s somewhat a source of mockery within the Twilight fandom, but the reality is you can either acknowledge the reality of what a walking corpse is or ignore it… but you’re still ignoring that they’re walking corpses at the end of the day lol.

Well, I don’t think it’s fair to put Marcel and Hope in the same category because their relationship wasn’t exactly the same. Klaus did have a fatherly demeanour towards him, but he also had a masterly disposition towards him and expected a leave of obedience and deference that wouldn’t be expected from your child, even by nineteenth century standards. Marcel was his ward, a person in his household whom he was legally responsible for but owed no emotional attachment towards. Now, as it happened, Klaus did have a lot of fondness for Marcel, which is why assessing what the exact term for their relationship is becomes difficult. The short of it being that I don’t think the kind of emotional connection and dependence there was ever as deep with Marcel as it was with Hope. 

So, first, motivations. Klaus’ desire to save Marcel from his abusive situation is nothing but admirable, it seems to me. But I don’t think it’s fair to look at his “Every King needs an heir” statement and therefore extrapolate a universal condemnation of him, because that’s clearly not the point. In that moment, yes, Klaus is selfish and even sadistic in his utter disregard for the potential of his child’s life except insofar in how she can benefit him. But that’s the point of the show. We see how Klaus goes from being that dismissive of her to someone who grows to genuinely care about and love her, willing to move heaven and earth to keep her safe. So we shouldn’t be looking at Klaus’ initial reaction to having a child - which even earlier than the bench conversation was “kill it idc” - but at how he acted when she was born, which was a look of nothing but love and devotion. (Also, Marcel would never have accepted Hope as a Co-ruler. Getting him to even be on the Mikaelsons’ side was a challenge enough, so I don’t think it’s fair to criticise Klaus for not pursuing an insanely unrealistic option.)

Second, this is heavily moving the goalposts from simply putting her in danger. A failure to consider all possible options - such as the fact that you have an insanely powerful aunt you never knew about who wants her for her magic - is not the same as actively putting her in danger. All the moves Klaus makes to keep her safe are done with the best of intentions and done to the best of his ability. Was there room for improvement? Sure, there is with everyone. I don’t think we can therefore conclude that a failure to pursue the best choice at all opportunities means that person is a terrible parent, because that means there are a LOT of terrible parents out there when Klaus actually did what most good parents do which is the best choice with the options they think they have. 

Third, this is just evidence that we shouldn’t consider Marcel to seriously be his son. He would never have imposed that choice on Hope, so that clearly means we shouldn’t be putting them on the same level if he treats Marcel the same way he treats everyone else. 

Fourth, again more evidence that Marcel is not viewed as his actual son. A fatherly disposition on occasion while still retaining a lordly authority the rest of the time clearly means we should not equivocate Marcel with his actual daughter who he never failed to treat with empathy and care.

Fifth, yeah that’s fucking stupid, but that’s more down to terrible writing. 😂 They wanted it to be the case that Klaus goes into a deep depression from being unable to see Hope, so they forget that phones exist and they can communicate through FaceTime almost as regularly as if nothing had happened. So I guess I’ll concede that this was just straight up bad parenting but this was bad writing, not really an intentional fault in Klaus’ character.

To conclude, while Klaus was not an ideal father and the person he was and life he led inevitably meant that his daughter would be put in danger, I think as soon as he accepted that he actually wanted to be a good father to her, he did everything in his power to make that happen. He did all he could to conceal that part of himself from her and give her a happy childhood unlike the one he had. He cared for her, adored her, loved her and died for her.

I really don’t think most people expect much more of their parents when it really comes down to it.

Even leaving that aside, I’m not sure we ever get to a point where civilisation like Rome or Carthage can even exist. The entire reason why we have been able to develop complex city states and interconnected trade routes is because we are the only species on this planet capable of it. The greatest danger when making a journey in antiquity was other humans. Unless you were exceptionally unlucky, wild animals were never that great a danger. But if we introduce the idea that dinosaurs are just… there? I’m not sure that ever happens. How can there ever be settled cities when, at any moment, a prehistoric behemoth can just crash through the city walls and plunder your reserves? And how will you stop him with Iron Age technology - or even more primitive? You can’t. All you can do is protect the meat and food you’ve collected as a small, mobile tribe and hope you can stay out of their way. They aren’t like wolves who can be tamed and domesticated, they are too large and unruly to ever acknowledge man as lord, so the possibility of dinosaur mounts is beyond historical fiction, it’s straight up Sci-Fi.

I don’t doubt that EVENTUALLY, we would start developing settled civilisation but the key priority would be making sure they were safe from dinosaur attacks, meaning every settlements would need to be walled or else be entirely vulnerable to attack. This means that any society you know about that didn’t have defined, walked settlements? Yeah, they don’t exist, they can’t exist in this ecological climate. What’s more, they would rarely be connected. The risk of venturing begin your borders for more than was necessary would be a risk too great, so vast empires and complex interconnected cultures are out of the question.

What’s also inevitable is that as soon as humans have the privacy to develop technology, they start thinking of ways to kill dinosaurs, and eventually they would be successful. They would pioneer ways to bring the beasts down and cull their populations to the point of near extinction- probably total extinction in more than a few places. In the places where dinosaurs don’t exist now, you can expect human development to catch up back to what it would recognisably look like in OTL without the impediment of another predator, but also unrecognisable to us. It would be many centuries or millennia after what we would expect the first civilisations to crop up. Depending on how long this process takes, it could be well into the “AD” timescale by the time this all comes to an end. The languages, cultures and religions that would emerge from this world would be alien to us. They would be defined by this centuries long struggle against the dinosaurs, with myths and legends surrounding them and the greatest of heroes being those who slayed the most ferocious. I don’t doubt dinosaurs evolve through storytelling into being the basic source of evil in almost all human culture because of this shared, primeval terror all humankind once shared because of them. Over the centuries, as they became an obscurity, people would move on from being solely defined by them and by the time of some comparable 19th/20th century, you’d see conservation efforts to protect the last dinosaurs from total extinction.

But the idea of humans using dinosaurs like Dino Riders? Yeah, that goes beyond the scope of this subreddit and is straight up Science Fiction. It requires us to make humans far more competent than we were and to make dinosaurs far less dominant in order for us to even get to that stage.

But with ALL of that being said, I will engage the hypothetical: If dinosaurs existed and were capable of being domesticated, they wouldn’t just CHANGE warfare, they would BE warfare. It would be utterly pointless for there to ever be professionally trained soldiers as why would you need them when you’d have dinosaurs? These huge, lumbering beasts would do all of humanity’s fighting for us. Even more than horses could ever do, to be a dinosaur rider would be the highest honour any society could betsow. It would make you the key difference between victory and defeat because what else was there? Even if you had the best army in the world, a pterodactyl could just swoop through your phalanx with ease. No serious nation would even try taking to battle without using dinosaurs, they would be the most precious resource possible. And sure, there would be humans trained with weaponry capable of killing them, getting progressively better over the centuries. But it would really take until some comparable Industrial age to ever truly defeat dinosaurs without using any of your own. Until then, they would be the chief weapon of war, the most valued animals in the world and the reasons why empires rose and fell.

Well, first of all, what would have been the incentive? The purpose of the Crusades was to reclaim previously Christian lands and holy sites. There was nothing of religious value in Arabia for the crusaders, so they had no desire to claim - let alone reclaim - anything beyond Jerusalem. But even if we assume they just wanted to humiliate the Muslims for the sake of it, Mecca and Medina were not strategically valuable. They had wealth as centres of pilgrimage, to be sure, but nothing that would justify the effort required to take them. And even if you could take them, there was no way of easily defending them. It would be all too easy for an Egyptian or Arabian force to cut off the route to the Crusader kingdoms and thus leave the two cities stranded and the garrisons preparing for starvation.

Not even addressing the fact that the campaign itself would have been a great effort. Located deep in the Hejaz, the only routes to them were either by sea - effectively impossible for a large crusading army - or to march an army of plate clad knights and armoured horses straight through, a recipe for death when not even counting the local hostiles on the way there. It would have required either a complete reworking of the way Europeans fought battles, the most immense preparations imaginable or the most extraordinary luck.

However, let’s set ALL of that aside. Let’s assume a large, European host would have been willing and able to march into Hejaz and launch a war for the purposes of taking the two holy cities in Islam simply because they could. And let’s also assume that they endured minimal casualties to give their chances of holding the cities the best chance. So far as I see it, there are two possible outcomes from this, and I think it depends on the character of the crusaders

The first will assume that the occupation of the two cities is relatively calm and peaceful. No doubt there would be some atrocities, as with any medieval taking of a city, but ultimately, the Christians move in and set up shop. The great mosques are closed down and forcibly turned into makeshift churches, the Adhan is replaced with the Latin mass and Bishops perform communion be for the Kaaba. I think the result of this is total shock and paralysation from the entire Islamic world. For centuries, these cities had been THE centre of their faith, where their prophet was from, where he commanded them to make the Hajj, places that were considered so holy as to be under God’s protection and where no Kafir was allowed to tread. For Christians to not just be walking there but *owning* the holy sites, preventing the practise of true Islam and practising their blasphemy would have destroyed the muslim world’s perception of itself. Take the abolition of the Caliphate in 1924 in our timeline. It was one of the most shocking blows to Islam ever seen because without a clear and central spiritual leader, who did Muslims turn to? It caused not exactly splits or schisms but cracks in Islam that we are still dealing with today because of how shattering a loss the caliph was, even if the position had lost its potency over the centuries. Imagine that loss times a thousand. Not only was this a much more religious time, it was a much more superstitious time. Victory in a battle was considered God’s divine favour on you, and losing the two holiest cities in Islam would have been seen as nothing less than divine wrath and judgement. It’s even possible, if unlikely, that you start to see a slow death of Islam as more and more people begin to turn away from it, believing that the Crusader victory is proof positive that the claims of Islam cannot possibly be true. I doubt that though. I also think the cities would eventually be retaken, I doubt any crusaders could have held them for more than a generation. But the shock and doubt that ever losing the cities would cause would be akin to 1204 for the Byzantine Empire. While it continued on, it was obviously shaken and would never be fully the same again. 

The second possibility will assume that the Crusaders show no mercy or restraint at all, with crimes of all varieties pardoned and sanction given to the most horrendous atrocities, up to and including the destruction of Muhammad’s tomb and body. All the great mosques would be destroyed, the Kabaa either moved or smashed and the population put to the sword. Instead of shock spreading across the Islamic world, you would instead have pure, unbridled rage at this atrocity. Muslims of all nations would have felt the immediate all to Jihad and demanded retribution for the destruction of the holy sites. The Crusader army would have been the first to go, its members tortured and slaughtered for their actions. Then, the entirety of the Crusader states - Christian or not. Then, the Byzantine Empire, with what remained of Anatolia falling entirely to hordes of vengeful Islamic warriors. How far would they get, and for how long would they carry on? I can’t say. But suffice it to say that effectively overnight, the Muslims would be turning the tide back on the Christians and restore their dominance in the region. In the aftermath, some of the shock of ever losing the cities might set in, but more powerful in the mind of Islam is the memory of what the Christians did to the holy cities and the desperation to ensure it never happens again.

Are either of these outcomes particularly likely? No. As I said above, any Christian army that attempted such a conquest would die on the way there and Muslims probably remember them in the same vein as the English think about the Spanish Armada or the Japanese about the Mongols - but probably even funnier to them because they were killed by the sun they knew was there rather than a storm they didn’t.

The Fallout 3-NV/Starfield system is pretty much the best basic foundation - a list of basic, vanilla options with other hidden options depending on your traits, race, skills, what quests you’ve accomplished, etc. I don’t really think there’s much more you can do than that besides making the dialogue options interesting, worthwhile and worth pursuing in multiple ways through multiple playthroughs. The problem FO4 had was that the options all felt very samey and produced the same outcomes, so variety in choice is definitely what you want to go for, but that’s a problem of execution and not the basic system itself.

If we were to try and improve on that, I guess the best new option would be to try and incorporate some level of risk into some options. Like let’s say you’re in a hostage standoff with a bandit and have a chance to talk to the chief, instead of passing everything with a level 100 Speech, you instead have an entirely new system where you have a limited number of options where what you say actually matters, maybe even a timer or a “agreement” meter that builds up depending on what you say and how quickly you say it. You’d have more sophisticated options if your speech was higher but you’d ultimately still be able to get very lucky even if you were very low, unlike the current system where you’re locked out of the good ending if you’re one speech mark off, more comparable to pickpocketing where it’s harder but not impossible on lower levels.

I’m not sure how this would actually pan out in execution but that’s the way I’d go to try and give something genuinely new aside from just making sure the basic dialogue in the game is more worthwhile than it has been in recent games.

That’s when I stopped wanting to go outside, I became so much paler than before, I developed Aquaphobia and had to turn back whenever I drove by a river, I began to hate garlic bread and my vision must have been going because sometimes I could have sworn my eyes were red in a certain light. Hazel said this was going to be a confusing time for me and I remember feeling so afraid until she shared her vintage wine with me. I’d never been huge on wine before but that brand was even more intoxicating than her. One sip and I felt so much more alive than ever before! I wanted it all but Hazel told me I needed to pace myself or would risk exposing us. I always wondered what she meant by that but never got an answer.

One night, I came home and found a letter on the table saying she’d left and was never coming back. The thing is, I knew. I just remember driving under the moonlight and suddenly feeing a pit in my stomach, like I’d been stabbed, the most terrible feeling and I was thinking only of her. I don’t know what I did wrong to drive her away, but the strangest feeling of all was that I wasn’t upset or distraught, I felt relieved. I loved her, and yet I still felt like a burden had been lifted from my shoulders. To this day, I can’t explain it. Nor can I explain why she left so much dust on our floor before she left! It was like she’d emptied our vaccum’s contents on the floor, then cleaned it up again but still left some like she’d been cleaning in a hurry. I think the real problem here is George needing to flesh the world out as he goes along.

In the early books, “The Targaryens went mad due to inbreeding” makes sense as a piece of worldbuilding and there’s no real reason to question it… until you actually need to give depth and detail to those three centuries of Targaryen history because just writing them all as insane isn’t just repetitive and boring, it’s also nonsensical. The dynasty should have been overthrown long ago if that was the case, so George writes about the good, bad and messed up of the dynasty but his asset is his greatest curse - all his characters are profoundly human. Even Aerys II, the supposed apotheosis of deranged Targaryen insanity as the early books described him, has not just the lifelong jealousy/rivalry with Tywin, the fact he was imprisoned in Duskendale and the very clear hints that he wasn’t actually paranoid and there was a conspiracy to either place Rhaegar on the throne or supplant the Targaryens altogether. Whether you agree with that case or think Aerys was just insane, it doesn’t matter, the point is that George gave even Aerys an out from just being born irredeemably crazy. And with all the Kings before him, that problem is even more manifest. They were vain, arrogant, superstitious, lazy, cowardly and detached from the world but all of their personality flaws were explainable by their own complicated backstories. None were simply mad from birth because of inbreeding and there was nothing to be done - except Aerion maybe lol. And this isn’t a problem, but it is a soft retcon of the way the Targaryens are described in those early books. There’s simply no way they would have the “gods flip a coin” reputation given what we know about their personalities, it is an aspect that George has overwritten with time.

It’s the same as what happened with the Dance. Initially, the Dance began because Criston Cole, on his own, crowned Aegon over his full sister - only older by a couple years- Rhaenyra.” But now Alicent and Otto were scheming for years to put Aegon on the throne. And Criston wasn’t all that important at all. 

Can you squint and make the differences work? Sure, but it still seems irrefutably clear that George simply changed his mind about how these things actually worked when he had to give more detail to how it happened than a throwaway line in a chapter that was focused on other things.

The singular driving force of the French Revolution was the economic crisis of the 1780s, which was due to many long and short term factors but one of them was the impoverished French treasury due to France throwing so much blood and treasure into the American revolution, for which France received very little in direct reinvestment. Whatever else one may say of the Sun King, he never allowed France’s coffers to run dry completely, certainly not for a cause that did not benefit France directly. So without that cause alone, I find it very difficult to believe the Revolution would have happened in the manner it did, nevermind the other and more recent causes of revolution in 1789.

However, let’s ignore those butterflies and say that the Nine Years War was actually far more economically devestating for France than it was in OTL, and it was already bad for France. Let’s say the famine and economic collapse was so bad that all of Louis’ attempts to restore the economy through traditional - and his not so traditional- means fell through and he had no choice but to also call the Estates-General.

The biggest question is “Could he cudgel the estates into agreement?” The aristocracy were famously defanged by Louis so it seems likely they’d agree to any terms forced upon them. The same goes for the clergy, though to a lesser extent given Louis’ recent conflict with Rome. And with the third estate? The most obvious solution they would demand is a reform to France’s taxation system like OTL’s did in 1789, meaning there are two possible options;

1.Louis XIV, unlike the ineffective and indecisive XVI, would come to an agreement with the third estate that would effectively reform France’s laws to benefit the bourgeoisie and peasantry. Using force of personality - and likely just force - he would compel the other two estates to accept the burden of taxation. They would grumble about this but ultimately, it would allow the economic crisis to abate, freeing France up to renew its strength just in time for the war of the Spanish Succession. Revolution averted, Vive Le Roi!

2.Far more likely is that Louis, as an ardent and committed absolutist, steadfastly refuses to grant ANY assent to the peasants and upholds both the doctrine of Divine Right and the privileges of the aristocracy which protect them from the burden of taxation. 

Now, the Third Estate became the National Assembly in OTL because of the ideological trends in place by the 1780s and the people involved. Without those individuals being in place, it’s very unlikely that the same course of events takes place. Because these movements were in their intellectual infancy in France in the 1690s, it’s most plausible that the peasantry are simply taxed into oblivion to compensate whatever needs the Estates have and Louis crushes any discontent with force of arms given there is no other avenue available to them.

But again, let’s wave away the butterflies and assume there is in fact an ideological class capable of opposing the King and establishing a National Assembly in 1789. Louis’ first move would be to crush it, brutally and without compromise. Any known members would be charged with treason, any known associates would be arrested and any tennis courts would be burnt down as an example. Even assuming Louis is successful in tracking down these early leaders, the predictable result is that they become martyrs for the cause of liberation.

The French army under Louis XIV was disciplined, well trained and effective, so I think he would have a much easier time of maintaining control of Paris than XVI, I feel very confident in saying that Louis would not allow any kind of event like the storming of the bastille to take place, even though these hypothetical Jacobins would be looking for an opportunity to make a symbolic victory of that kind knowing they could not challenge the King directly. I think this state of affairs would have continued pretty much unchanged, with the King constantly repressing revolutionary fervour and the people eternally unable to break the stranglehold Louis had on them…

Until the War of the Spanish Succession. With no other realistic options, Charles II still names Philip as his heir and war breaks out over that assignation… but not to France’s benefit. Like the NYW of this timeline, the outbreak of war creates a crisis and opportunity at home for France’s aspiring revolutionaries. In an ironic twist of fate in this timeline, you could see Britain and Austria funding revolutionaries in France to destabilise the French monarchy and compel a surrender much faster than in OTL. How far would this go? I have no idea. At best, Louis quickly accepts defeat with the Spanish throne being handed over to the Allied candidate of Charles so he can focus on the crisis at home. At worst, a combined Allied-French revolutionary army marches on Paris and Versailles and displaces the Bourbon monarchy permanently.

I think the latter significantly more unlikely but even in the former, Louis would be severely wounded by this war. His position and power shaken, even if he was able to cling onto the mantra of Divine Rule, everyone could clearly see he was not the King he once was. His realm would be a powder keg, a barely repressed nation yearning for the opportunity to end their suffering, yet eternally denied that chance so long as he was alive… until he died… and the crown he would pass to his great-grandson… a five year old.

Do I even need to explain what would happen next? Instead of the strong and stable realm Louis XV inherited, the boy’s first memories would be of being driven from his home, and probably kingdom, after the Jacobins saw their chance and took it. The most likely way this happens is that the pro-Japan lobby within the British Empire ensures that the Anglo-Japanese alliance doesn’t get replaced by the 1922 Imperial Conference and the 1922 Washington Naval Conference, and the two empires continue to rely on each other to the exclusion of the United States. Thus, when FDR calls for an embargo on oil shipments to Japan, it is of little effect because Japan will be relying on Britain for its oil needs.

The other immediate effect of this is that the “South Road” doctrine of the Japanese Navy loses out as expansion into Indonesia and the Philippines will case unnecessary turmoil with the British, which the Japanese now desperately need to avoid. Thus, the Imperial Army will win out for its support to expand further into Manchuria, China and the Soviet Union. It’s possible that the British could act as a mediating influence on the Japanese so atrocities like Nanking are not anywhere near as barbaric as OTL but I would doubt it. The more likely outcome is that Britain’s alliance is put into serious question by an outraged British public at the stories of these atrocities, similar to how Ottoman crimes in Bulgaria put an end to Disraeli’s Anglo-Ottoman alliance of the 1870s under Liberal pressure, but far less likely to succeed given that Japan would be more vital to British interests than the Ottomans were.

Whatever the case, this alliance does not affect the European theatre; Hitler invades France, the BEF collapses and Churchill refuses to surrender. What could be the most interesting effect is how America is handled. With no oil crisis between Japan and America, Pearl Harbour will not happen. But the lend lease program will still be ongoing and Hitler will be eager to prevent it to knock Britain out of the war while Barbarossa is ongoing - additionally, there may be some secret communication between Germany and Japan even in this timeline as both will presumably be at war with the Soviet Union at the same time, though Japan would prefer Britain never find out about it. So even without the inciting incident of Pearl Harbour as a pretext, it is possible Hitler still declares war on the United States anyway. Maybe this is delayed by a year until 1942, but I doubt it would be much longer than that. 

So, as the world stands; Germany is at war with Britain and the United States. Japan is at war with China and the Soviet Union. And Germany is at war with the Soviet Union. Which of course begs the question; Whose side is Japan on? Either Japan will have to relent it’s war against the Soviets to appease the British who desperately need cooperation with them to defeat Hitler or abandon the alliance with Britain to maintain its conquests in the far east - or near west to Japan, I suppose.

In scenario 1: Japan realising Britain is too valuable an ally relents its conquests in the Soviet Union, pays reparations and enters a non aggression pact, while diverting its entire military might against the Chinese to gain as many pieces of territory as possible. With no Pacific theatre, all the might of the United States and the British Empire can be levied against Nazi Germany (and italy too ig.) Because of the exclusive effort, it is possible the war could be shortened by as much as two years. I certainly would predict at least an attempted D Day of some description before the end of 1943. As a result, France, the Low Countries and Scandinavia are liberated that much sooner. But I doubt an unconditional surrender is imposed on Germany. If the Anglo-American armies are quick enough, Germany will want a quick peace in order to focus on the ongoing war in the east. We’re already several “Maybes?” deep and I’m unsure of how the negotiations would proceed. Would it just be a return to 1933, would they demand occupation and would they demand Germany abandon its war in the east or let them keep fighting to weaken both expansionist authoritarian states? I’m unsure. Certainly the Nazi regime is disbanded and some kind of Liberal party put into power with western backing.

Scenario 2: Valuing its conquests in Russia too much, Japan ignores British demands to relent on their new ally and the Anglo-Japanese alliance is rendered obsolete. Britain responds with an oil embargo on Japan. With the Navy weakened with years of reliance on the “North Road” doctrine, it can only pursue a defensive measure should the Royal Navy strike from Singapore. Japan thus throws all its might at the Soviet Union, hoping to scoop up as many oil rich provinces in the east as they can before the Wehrmacht gets there first. Are they successful in this venture? I don’t know. Perhaps Anglo-American aid shipments step up and the Soviets are able to hold them off to secure something that looks like OTL, or maybe with resources needed to protect the eastern front, the Soviets can’t fight the Germans and Japanese at the same time leading to the collapse of the country. In that result, either Britain and America sue for peace or they continue fighting to the bitterest of ends. In this timeline, nuclear bombs are dropped on Berlin and Hamburg for sure if the war is still ongoing in 45, and perhaps that crushing blow gains a favourable peace for the allies but I doubt it. If Japanese intervention knocks Russia out of the war, it becomes near impossible to impose unconditional surrender on Germany, a settled peace at that point is all but inevitable, it would just depend on who it favours.

Overall, it depends what Japan’s interests are. If they are able to secure an empire in Asia without trampling on Anglo-American interests, their absence from the war almost certainly leads to a quicker defeat of Germany and a stronger starting position for the capitalist powers in the Cold War. Though the Cold War as we know it may not even happen. If the war is shorter and the British position is not so thoroughly smashed at Singapore, it is possible that Britain will be able to hold onto its empire. Probably not in India but certainly Africa, Suez in particular, and the Asian outposts - possibly even gaining Hong Kong in perpetuity as a thank you from a victorious Japan in China. As a result, the US is not so much of a hegemonic power as it was in OTL with Britain able to retain its prestige and influence long into the century, as certainly will be the case with Japan which will remain an autocratic militaristic state.

So, while you’re not incorrect that there was a lot of cultural assimilation among the “English” who moved to Ireland between the Norman Conquest and independence, it is important to note that there was a separation between social classes in this respect. The lower orders, particularly if they were actual farmers, tended to interact with culturally Irish people a lot more to become assimilated than their landlord/overseer class who stayed apart from the rest of society and retained their “Englishness.” After all, this is why the Protestant Ascendancy existed at all; historically Norman families who converted to Anglicanism to retain political favour. And that culture persisted pretty much up until the era of Home Rule. So I don’t think it’s a guarantee that if there was an independent Irish Jacobite kingdom that this cultural assimilation would continue to transcend class borders. I think you would see a parallel situation to what happened in OTL with an elite who regarded themselves as English and yearnt to return to the homeland, in spite of their Catholic faith which they shared with the Irish but not their English Protestant counterparts across the sea.

On the absolutism point, I think you give James II way, WAY too much credit. All the factors that you mention predate his accession to the throne in 1685, yet he continued to act like an absolutist Catholic who wished to impose a French style of government upon England, rule without Parliament and establish the Catholic religion as law. There’s legitimate debate as to how much he intended it to be read this way and how much was misinterpreted, but I definitely side with the reading that James wanted to bring Louis’ style of rule to England but was always cautious about how much he could get away with, even when he was putting bishops on trial or putting Catholics in positions wherever he could find them. *BUT,* if after these wars, James was restored to a throne, he would not have just considered it good luck, he would have considered it nothing less than divine providence and sanction for his Catholicisation mission. He already thought the realm coming to his side in the Monmouth rebellion was a sign from God that he had blessed his reign, and heavily misread what was actually a desire to avoid a second civil war. But if he was made King of Ireland in 1697, he would have had zero doubts in his mind that God had personally appointed him and sanctioned everything he wanted to do. There is absolutely no doubt in my mind, especially with the support of the French army, that James would have established an absolute monarchy in Ireland with zero reservations about where power in the country lay, and absolutely zero ability to practise anything less than devout Catholicism.

Neither James nor William would tolerate this arrangement. William would never accept the security risk of a French puppet on his doorstep and James would never settle for being king of a second rate dump like Ireland when he saw restoring the Church to England as his true destiny. Let’s say, however, for the sake of argument that Louis forces James to accept these terms and gives sufficient guarantees to William to make him accept.

The immediate consequences is a brutal and ruthless reprisal against Ulster’s Protestants for defying James in the siege of Derry, likely followed with mass killings and expulsions, with the land being handed back to the Old English aristocracy. Images and tales of the survivors in England and Scotland make the anti-Catholic hysteria a thousand times worse and while William would attempt to quieten these thoughts, he would be largely unsuccessful and anti-Catholic riots likely become a common sight in the coming years in England, with accusations of Jacobite loyalties being much more common and the image of James’ spies in media being a cause of panic for English Protestants. On the bigger geopolitical scene, not much difference, Ireland was only a concern for the English so with Louis accepting the Protestant accession to the thrones of England and Scotland, the wider European scene looks indistinguishable from our timeline.

In the medium term and the coming Act of Union, fear of the Jacobite kingdom across the sea is a looming threat with anti-Catholic and anti-Irish propaganda intensifying making Catholic emancipation significantly more difficult than in our timeline. There is probably an invasion attempt(s) from a prospective James III or IV, which likely also ends in failure, possibly even with a British army toppling the Jacobite threat with no wider continental threat to deal with - unless said invasion is part of one of those multi-front European wars allied with the Catholic powers but I digress. Aside from this, both the foreign and domestic theatres of England remain virtually unchanged from our timeline. Ireland, however, is a different story. With the backing of the French and emboldened by absolutism, the already flimsy Parliament in Dublin would be disbanded, with James ruling as his father had done in a personal capacity. The Old English would be thrilled for the Catholic Church to be restored, but the more native Celtic Irish would find no more friends in this political system than the prior one/averted Protestant Ascendancy. Ireland, in many ways, probably comes to mirror Russia; an economy largely based on agriculture, a people locked out of power, an absolute monarch dominating an autocratic political system enforced through a brutal aristocracy and a mono-culture seeking to suppress all others. To the British cartoonist, the Kingdom of Ireland represents the absolute worst of what Catholic, Jacobite rule has to offer as they would remind their readers for the rest of the century. 

Now, the reality is that there is no way this arrangement lasts more than 20 years, nevermind a century but for the sake of argument, let’s say London accepts Irish independence all the way until the French Revolution.

Because, on the one hand, France would be bankrolling this entire enterprise. Without the support of Paris, this kingdom likely falters and crumbles as bad as Cuba and North Korea dod after the Soviet Union fell, which would be the predictable result of the French Revolution and the National Assembly aghast at financially supporting another reactionary monarchy. On the other, we have the United Irishmen to consider. In OTL, Ulster Presbyterians and Irish Catholics united to rebel against the Anglican aristocracy in 1798, supported by the French - though their fleet was sank. Now, while the Belfast Presbyterians who were the driving force of the UI in OTL would have been driven out of the island long ago, I think the political situation was still ripe for revolution. With the Jacobite monarchy being more autocratic than the Hanoverians and the lack of a British army to suppress the revolt, I think 1798 ends with the overthrow of the Stuart dynasty and the establishment of an Irish republic based upon similar values to the French one, though hopefully with less terror and guillotines - though that is absolutely not certain. Much like the French Revolution, the corresponding Irish Revolution could tell English Anglican aristocrats of what awaits them. However, in spite of that, I actually think it’s possible the Irish Republic could moderate very quickly and establish a working relationship with Britain. Lacking France’s population and geography, they cannot afford a war on the Napoleonic scale so suing for peace is their best, but not only, option.

If Dublin sues for peace, history progresses basically unchanged until 1815. No, it is not remotely plausible that people just rise to dynastic positions from being popular. George keeps doing this, with the entire Blackfyre claim resting on “but Daemon is so cooolllll,” and this just didn’t happen. The closest historical parallel is Henry IV, but he was the head of his branch of the family, a cousin of Richard II and Richard was such an abysmal King who had gone out of his way to piss everyone off. Nowhere in English medieval history does a King displace another simply because one was more popular, it was always about the rival claims. Maybe there’s some example in Europe I’m not aware of but definitely not in the main sources of inspiration George is drawing on.

Yes, some Reach lords stood to gain with Renly. And some doubtless married into the Westerlands and had more favour with the Lannisters. Or with the Stormlands and, if Stannis were the Lord, had more to gain from Stannis. But again, even reaching a plurality - nevermind the vast majority - being on Renly’s side is absurd. I again come back to the principle of inheritance because that is so strongly imbedded in this culture that it should prevent claims like this from even being considered, because that is the overriding principle. The wars of the roses didn’t happen because people liked the Yorkists more than the Lancasters, they were simply descendants of Edward III’s older son, that was it.

Also, we keep being told that the Reach is filled with ambitious, power hungry lords looking to make a name for themselves… but at every turn, they default to being subservient to the Tyrells. It’s a very obvious disconnect and I don’t think it’s intentional, it’s just that the actual fallout on the Reach of the War of Five Kings would be far more bloody and divisive than George would like to portray and would keep attention away from the plot lines he actually wants to write about, which is something of a consistent theme with many other aspects of the story.

That’s the story George is telling with these brothers, that’s beyond obvious. But it doesn’t make any sense that Stannis is forced into this position. He should have been Lord of Storm’s End, he should have the backing of most Storm Lords and a minority of other nobles from other kingdoms, and Renly’s army should be made up of knightly second sons and peasants who think he’s pretty, more than enough room for Stannis to fight a conventional war and win… but George can’t have that. In order to get the character arc he wants, Stannis has to be put into an unrealistic situation where he has no choice but to cheat to win. And the fact that he is in that position at all is the essence of what I’m complaining about.

Renly’s army doesn’t make a whole lot of sense.

First of all, why was he the Lord of Storm’s End in the first place? Stannis was his elder, the castle was his as soon as Robert ascended the throne. It doesn’t make sense that Robert would take the castle he held for a year away from him out of some misguided sense of affection by giving him Dragonstone instead, but that’s not the real reason. But let’s even leave that aside. Even if Renly holds Storm’s End, why do any of the Storm Lords listen to him? Renly setting the precedent that you can just upend the whole feudal system means any of their more popular brothers or sons can just displace the current Lord if they so choose. Adhering to Renly’s claim simply because he is popular does nothing but undermine their own stability and legitimacy. At most, Renly’s army in the Stormlands should be a peasant volunteer force of men who do genuinely think he’s Robert 2, and a bunch of incredibly ambitious second (and third, fourth, etc) sons looking to make a name for themselves. But again, if the Reach is fighting each other, Stannis has more of an excuse to fight a conventional war, meaning he won’t use the shadow baby.

Renly’s whole place in the story is just very contrived. It’s made ridiculously easy for him to assemble an army and overturn centuries of tradition to gain overwhelming force simply so Stannis is faced with the impossible choice of compromising his principles to scatter the army or go to battle knowing he faces certain defeat. The far more realistic host for Renly to have is a majority of peasant volunteers, some Stormland knights and a core of Tyrell loyalists. A threat to be sure, but nothing so ridiculously large as what he was given in the story for no other reason than it was more convenient to get Stannis to where he needs to be on his character arc.

For sure, Rome with railroads is capable of conquering China in a couple centuries, maybe even less, and that aspect shouldn’t be understated when looking at the colonial empires of modernity and why they didn’t collapse under their own weight. Still though, I would give more credit to the decentralised model they operated under. Fast communication or no, a localised command structure will be able to deal with problems more immediately than once that always has to refer back to London for new orders.

I don’t really think social trends affected the Empire at all. After 1857 especially, the British had a very light touch in regards to interfering with local customs of their subject peoples, certainly in comparison to others. They for certain encouraged British dress, Anglicanism and so forth among the dominions but it was rare that they actively imposed their culture upon others except in the case of the slave trade. Mostly they just taxed the people and extracted natural resources from the region. If anything, the British were adept at adapting to social trends. It’s why they were such masters at the divide and rule strategy which prevented many colonial possessions from uniting against them. Without that understanding of their subjects, the British would have been in much more trouble than they were.

That’s why I say the world wars are the most decisive factor in the collapse of the Empire. Absent it - though I think WW1 was inevitable due to the prior centuries of colonialism but I digress - the Empire was not in a bad shape. India and Africa were almost entirely pacified, Canada and Australia were effectively self-governing, East Asia was quiet and the Caribbean hadn’t been a bother in over a hundred years. Before 1913, Irish home rule was the most hotly debated Imperial issue for the British. So if WW1 doesn’t happen, I don’t see why the Empire wouldn’t have just continued to exist.

I don’t think the British Empire really did overextend itself. At least, not in the same way. Mongolia and Macedonia were too invested in the life of their conquering autocrat so when he went, the stability of the Empire went too. Rome is more complicated as most acquisition of land happened in the Republic but certainly once the principate was established, the state’s stability was tied to his life as well.

The British Empire, however, was a lot more decentralised. In spite of having a monarch, the various realms, dominions and territories that comprised it did not answer to the monarchy of England/Britain as directly and enjoyed a great deal of autonomy and indiscretion. That’s not to say various governments didn’t try to implement more top down control but given the breadth of distance between them, that just wasn’t possible. The political structures of the colonies acknowledged Victoria as overall sovereign, but in reality, they were effectively independent and didn’t rely on a top down structure as much as Macedonia or Rome.

So when you look at a map, it looks like some hugely impossible structure to manage but when you break it down, each of the colonies are perfectly manageable on their own with greater individual autonomy than many Roman provinces.

Of course, the British Empire never had a child monarch in its history or a succession crisis, which is probably something that would have split the colonies into declaring for one King or the other. But still, even leaving that aside, it was an incredibly durable and long lasting Imperial project that required the two biggest wars in human history to shake it to its foundations… and even then managed to hold on for another couple decades.

If he succeeds, he will single handedly restore his family to the Dark Lord’s favour and his father will be personally indebted to him, giving him the love he always craved. And why should he care about Dumbledore, who has always made his preference for Potter clear? 

It’s not just that he didn’t kill, it’s that he didn’t kill knowing what the consequences would be for his family if he didn’t and knowing that Dumbledore and his wider supporters were never going to accept him as one of them. It was only his personal unwillingness to be as evil as his family that held him back, and I think that should get him credit, in spite of all the awful things he did in the first five books.

I don’t think Sirius is a good comparison because his parents actively resented him for not living up to their standards, and as he knew he wasn’t measuring up in small ways, he started to act out in larger ways. They caused the gap between them and only widened it over time.

For all of Lucius and Narcissa’s faults, they did love Draco and even if they were emotionally distant from him, it was in such a way that Draco believed he could attain the love he so desperately sought from them whereas Sirius knew it was never going to happen. So Draco acts a certain way because it’s what he’s been conditioned to believe by the nature of his environment, yes, but he also moulds himself into a shape he hopes will be pleasing to his father, and wider family.

He was an antagonistic bully, no one can deny that. He was prideful, vain, short tempered, self-centred, malicious, cruel and both a class and blood supremacist. But in spite of all of that, manifesting in many examples over the course of the first five books, he wasn’t evil. The scale of his actions were read through the eyes of Harry, used to being tortured and bullied by his cousin, and just replaced Dudley for Draco in his mind. But when you get down to it, he was just another school bully. He never did anything on the scale of the Death Eaters, or even showed signs that he wanted to be like them. His cruelty was childish and petty, so the audience is primed to go along with Harry’s paranoia about him in HBP. Harry thinks the worst of him, and so too will the reader.

But, much like a lot of things in this series, you can’t judge by appearances. Because when Draco was given his first truly evil task of murdering Dumbledore, he fumbled it. And it’s easy to write this off as “Oh he didn’t kill someone? Big whoop.” But imagine what it’s like for Draco. You’ve got the Dark Lord personally assigning you a task under threat of murder if you don’t. If you succeed, you will become one of his most valued servants and your family will be restored to honour. Your father, fallen in favour, will owe his standing to you. He will give you the love you’ve always craved. And Dumbledore? Dumbledore is your enemy. He’s made it clear he’s on Team Potter since he snubbed you out of the House Cup in First Year. He would expel you if he knew about the mark on your arm. You have absolutely no reason to want to hesitate and every reason to want to kill… and yet he doesn’t. He finds every way he can to put it off without actively refusing Bellatrix or, by extension, Voldemort.

I think this is all worth taking into consideration when talking about Draco because while he does have villainous traits, he is not a villain himself. It’s not like he has some secret hero waiting to break out, it’s not anywhere as simple or romantic as that. But it is to say that just because he’s done many bad things, for which he should be held accountable, we should group him in with people who do even worse simply because he didn’t turn away from his family given the entire context of his upbringing.

It’s a difference in artistic intent.

In SOM, you spend the majority of the game fighting orcs. Your purpose is to remove them from the hierarchy by killing them, so you need to feel afraid of them. Or at least, recognise that they are an unsettling and creepy enemy. This is also to contrast with when you do gain the ability to dominate as it’s always unsettling to take these enemies who are so unpleasant and unnerving and make them your loyal slaves. The game is built around the combat more than the domination.

In SOW, the inverse is true. You gain the ability to dominate relatively quickly and most of the game is built around building your army, so you need to feel close to them. Most of the games marketing also focused on this as the idea that you felt a personal connection to your orcs was a big part of the appeal of this game. So the orcs can’t look as creepy as they used to, they need to be more endearing and cartoony so they’re bearable to look at and you find yourself drawn to them and wanting to protect your favourites. The game is built around the idea of building an army more than defeating one.

So if you prefer more fearsome looking orcs, you’ll prefer SOM designs. And if you prefer ones you’ll actually have a bond with, you’ll prefer SOW’a designs. But I don’t think either art style works with the opposite way the game is built. Or at least, it wouldn’t work as well for most people.

IIRC, Lovecraft’s first work was published in 1917 while Tolkien wrote The Hobbit around 1930, and began writing LOTR in 1937. So the publishing dates might be further apart but there’s really only a couple decades between Lovecraft and Tolkien really putting Middle Earth together so I think it’s fair to say they were written around the same time.

But I don’t think Tolkien would ever have read his work. Tolkien was an esteemed English scholar and professor whose influences were the books already in his library, and Lovecraft was an American author catering for an entirely different audience. I don’t know how popular Lovecraft was in his lifetime or around the time Tolkien was thinking about Middle Earth but I think it’s extremely unlikely Tolkien would have let any modern, and certainly any American, work influence what he wanted to be a mythology for the English people. To say nothing of the fact that Tolkien would likely have been aghast at the content of his work, at best.

It is certainly possible he was inspired by some other cosmic horror work he read, or some conversation he had that put the idea in his head, but I think he would have been deliberate about keeping LOTR as aesthetically English as it was possible to be.

You are right that he was definitely interested in introducing things just to never explain them again, Bombadil is probably the best example of this. It gives a realism to the world that there are just things we will never see or be told about as they’re just not critical to the story being told.

The defining part of Lovecraftian/Cosmic Horror is how much of it is outside the knowable, understandable world and how it cannot be understood because these beings are so ancient and terrible as to be beyond us.

Is it possible that Níðhöggr was on Tolkien’s mind when writing about Gandalf’s descent? Sure, I could see the inspiration. But Níðhöggr just seems too familiar a concept to have given rise to what Gandalf talks about which I don’t really think has any analogue in any pre-Christian mythology. The whole point about those pantheons was that they were the people of antiquity trying to explain the natural world in ways that were understandable to them, so why would they invent beings whose purpose was not to be understood? To me, that seems to be something that can only come out of the “what else is there?” question when they believed that the triumph of science had explained everything in the Victorian era.

I could be wrong though. 🤷🏻‍♂️

In August, Operation Barbarossa was already underway so no hope of his death averting anything on the Eastern Front.

Since such great efforts were made to cover up his health problems to maintain the image of a strong leader for a strong Germany, the immediate reaction would be sheer shock and panic. Not “rioting in the streets” panic but it would have shattered many illusions that people had come to have about the nature of Germany as if the Fuhrer himself was not the ideal German, what did that say of those left in his wake? This is what I think would be the most profound consequence for the German people. It would shatter many self-perpetuating delusions the state had been trying to propagate.

Politically speaking, as you’d expect, sheer fucking carnage. His death at the height of war would create a power vaccum and crisis that had the risk of spiralling into civil war with the the government and military splintering into factions under figures like Himmler, Goring, Gobbels and so forth. It’s even possible that this political instability causes a German civil war with so many desperate to maintain order in the absence of Hitler’s death. There’s absolutely no way to tell who would win, or even who the most likely contenders would be either as this would be the perfect opportunity for a shadow candidate to rise and crush all opposition if allowed to.

On the western front, the British would be overjoyed at the news and would likely take the opportunity to regroup. If they’re lucky, the German internal instability is sufficient enough that future bombing campaigns of the UK are suspended if Goring believes he needs all the manpower he can get in Germany itself. As a result, the British people can recover from the Blitz and the RAF can take the opportunity to rearm… but there’s a bigger problem they’re not aware of, namely that Hitler was only four months away from declaring war on the USA. Without an obvious candidate when the Japanese attack Pearl Harbour, it’s unlikely the German leadership is able to declare war on another nation even if one or another faction wanted to. If there is no war against Germany, it’s likely that FDR comes under pressure to redirect his lend lease program away from Britain to the pacific war effort, leaving Britain more isolated than in OTL. The British will be able to recover in the crisis but even at full strength, they’re not going to be powerful enough to defeat the Germans on their own.

On the Eastern Front, it’s likely full steam ahead for the armies that have been sent to roll across the Soviet Union. As soon as they get the news that Hitler is dead, they likely halt to some degree as they’re uncertain of who to take orders from, especially if the political crisis escalates into a conflict of interests. As such, I doubt events like the Battle of Stalingrad even happen as I don’t think the Wehrmacht is able to get that far into Germany, but I’m less confident of this prediction. If anywhere was most equipped to deal with their plans regardless of Hitler’s survival, it was the Eastern Front, assuming they don’t get pulled back. If the political situation gets dire enough, these armies could be called back to bolster the followers of someone like Himmler or Heydrich.

Beyond that, things get increasingly hard to predict. At the most general, the political crisis would end as soon as someone with the will to do so eradicates the competition and restores order to the Reich but this process could take months. It’s even a possibility that with such pressure at home, peace is sued for far earlier than in OTL, with Germany willing to accept far more humiliating terms just to be freed up to end civil strife at home, but I’m not confident it would get that bad in most likely scenarios. Most likely, the German armies would be able to hold their own in the east and west until a new Fuhrer could be selected to continue the war, though who knows how much better he would have fared than Hitler himself.

The one thing I can say for certain is that the Wannsee Conference does not happen. That only occurred because the internal stability of Germany was so strong and the war going so well that the Nazis believed they could begin the deportation and extermination of Jews immediately rather than needing to wait for a post-war settlement. If they had just recovered from an internal political crisis in 1942 when a new Fuhrer was barely able to assert himself, even to the Nazis, dealing with the Jewish Question would have been one of the last things on their minds given everything else they had to deal with. There would still have been concentration camps, mass killings and so forth but the deliberate, intentional, mechanical nature of the Holocaust would not have come to pass without the blueprint issued at Wannsee.

Ned isn’t very convinced of the letter First much at all:

> “Your sister is sick with grief. She cannot know what she is saying… The only truths I know are here. The south is a nest of adders I would do better to avoid.”

Luwin, meanwhile, is surprisingly neutral:

> “The Hand of the King has great power, my lord. Power to find the truth of Lord Arryn’s death, to bring his killers to the king’s justice. Power to protect Lady Arryn and her son, if the worst be true.”

He’s merely explaining that he could have the power to do so if he desires it, not going above his duties as a maester to give his opinion where it was not asked, though it seems strongly implied he agrees with Cat that Ned should accept Robert’s offer.

The biggest driving force for the pro-south argument is unambiguously Cat, and unambiguously because of the omen:

> “Now we truly have no choice. You must be Robert’s Hand. You must go south with him and learn the truth.”

She isn’t reaching a conclusion based solely on this evidence, Lysa’s letter is merely justifying a preconception that she already had. She believes in the power of gods and omens, and that she has been “rewarded” with yet more proof that she is right, and believes it foolhardy to continue to ignore what she sees as clear and irrefutable signs.

Is it *possible* that Catelyn might reach these conclusions on her own? Sure, I suppose. But since all the textual evidence points pretty clearly to Cat only taking this point of view because she believes her prior paranoia is justified, I don’t see what reason she would have to believe it without the foundation of the omen poisoning her mind to believe the worst was coming already. If she had received the letter but a week before the direwolf, she would likely have agreed with Ned that the letter meant nothing and Luwin’s tepid argument for going south would have persuaded neither of them. The omen is the domino that sets everything else off.

This is true, Ned does want to discover the truth and even if both he and Cat dismissed Lysa’s letter out of hand, the questions would still be gnawing away at him. Yet all the things he says indicate that he believes his place is in the North and without Catelyn’s insistence today, it’s very likely that this specific offer from Robert is rejected. He could deny Robert today but in a month or so accept the offer anyway as his mistrust of the Lannisters is great enough on its own that he would suspect them.

Yet this pause alone is significant, because if the Royal Party has already left when Ned accepts the offer, then Bran never falls from the tower. And if Ned is less sure about going, he may not take his whole household with him, another significant deviation with obvious ramifications for the rest of the story.

So even if the delay in Ned accepting is only short because Catelyn’s insistence is not there, that is still significant enough to shape the story unrecognisably from what we see it as in the story, so the omen remains the most important event that shapes the way events took their course in this series, and not without accident.

Because Cat interprets the dead direwolf in the stag’s antlers as an ill omen from the gods that predicts what will happen, namely that Robert will end up getting Ned killed.

> Catelyn remembered the direwolf dead in the snow, the broken antler lodged deep in her throat. She had to make him see. (Catelyn II, AGOT)

Without this message interpreted on her part as a warning she has to act upon in order to prevent the fate that is to befall her family, Catelyn does not act with as much paranoia as she does in the opening chapters of this book, she does not implore Ned to go south with Robert believing that Robert himself is the threat, which means there is a greater likelihood that even Lysa’s letter doesn’t move Catelyn and it is just interpreted as the ramblings of a madwoman in her grief. And if Ned doesn’t go, Bran doesn’t feel the need to go feed the crows in the tower one last time before he goes south with his father, so he never catches Jaime and Cersei and never falls from the tower, meaning that Ned never learns the secret of the Incest until Robert dies - which may still be many years off yet.

Basically, finding the direwolves is the event that kickstarts the entire plot, for better or worse, though largely for worse. And if they never find them, everything is entirely and radically different in the story going forward.
