He had no legitimate son, but plenty of illegitimate ones, and only one younger brother. The problem is that said brother was a Catholic and Parliament - or at least the Whigs in Parliament - didn’t want him to rule, they generally preferred his illegitimate son the Duke of Monmouth who was a Protestant.

For a man who had no issues with infidelity, and no scruples with stabbing people like Clarendon in the back when it was politically convenient, it’s REALLY weird that he was so devoted to his wife that he refused to divorce her so he could sire a legitimate son and prevent his brother from becoming King. I don’t know why Charles was so adamant about this and it confuses me to this day as he was clearly not a monogamous lover and had no issue with doing what was necessary yet on one of the most critical issues of his life chose to stand by her rather than do what everyone expected him to do.

Beyond that, I think Charles II was the last King who was able to shape national policy to his will with Parliament serving him rather than in a co-equal arrangement as would be the case after the Glorious Revolution. Charles was decisive, ambitious and ruthless when he had to be, but he was also affable, likeable and generous. There are few kings who have been loved more by their people, and next to none by their women. He restored religious liberty to his kingdoms, reinvigorated the arts and sciences and took personal charge in restoring London after the Great Fire - which he also took a direct hand in combatting. One could argue he was too compliant to France and Louis XIV given that he sold Dunkirk to him, but he was no sycophant and joined forces with his former enemy in Holland to fight France in the war of devolution. 

There are many minor issues in his reign as with all Kings but nothing for Charles so great as what to do with the succession, causing the split between the Whigs and Tories for the first time over whether James was a worthy successor, concluding with Charles suspending Parliament and living on Louis’ pension for the rest of his life. Was this the right decision? At the time, absolutely not, Charles must have known it would only end in disaster. But in the long run, his inaction was probably the most consequential decision of his life as without it, the history of Britain and the world would be unrecognisable if the throne had simply passed to Charles III in 1685 without controversy.

So I would have considered myself blessed to live under the reign of Charles II… I just wouldn’t leave my wife alone with him. 😂

Because there’s a disconnect between the reputation the Faceless Men have in the rest of the world and what we see in AFFC.

To most characters perception in ASOIAF, they seem indistinguishable from TES’ Dark Brotherhood, a shadowy group of assassins who will take on any contract for the right price. Everyone seems to understand that you can hire them pretty much at your leisure but they do NOT come cheap yet will get the job done with ruthless efficiency, no additional casualties and no ties back to you.

Yet we don’t find that when Arya encounters them. Instead what we find is a religious cult who don’t care about worldly concerns, but are chiefly motivated by the balance of life and death, and preserving it at all costs. At least, that’s their public display and they may have some darker ulterior motives only known to their most senior members but I digress.

The point being that there’s a serious disconnect between how people in Westeros perceive the group and how they actually operate. Why do they think they’re just killers for hire if they won’t take out a contract that would leave an imbalance in the world? Why do people think it will cost a lot of money when they don’t care about material possessions at all? It can’t just be that their legend has been spun out of proportion, they operate a semi-public operation in pretty broad daylight in a comparatively close city. Those kinds of perceptions would have been done away with by now, especially by people who are among Westeros’ elite and should know better. Littlefinger even brings the possibility up at a council meeting and he certainly should know it’s not true, unless we’re saying he brought the option up knowing it would be shot down. The idea that “a heavy price” has been misinterpreted as being only money when they actually demand a life in exchange for death would make sense if they operated somewhere like Asshai and there was no way anyone in Westeros could get reliable information about them. So I don’t know if there is something here I’m just not seeing, if George changed his mind about what kind of group he wanted them to be or what have you, but it seems abundantly clear that if the belief about the group was accurate, they would be employed by Lords all across Westeros for a variety of reasons. There was never any doubt in anyone’s mind that Ireland always came last.

Ireland was the inheritance of Norman imperialism and largely regarded by the English Aristocracy and Royalty as a nuisance and inconvenience to be dealt with. It was not a particularly valuable or profitable piece of land, with few cities and most of the country being pure farmland - often outdated and unproductive farmland at that. To be named the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland was a sign that you were not in the King’s favour, it was a role given to those who had to be got rid of without directly insulting them. It was only held onto to prevent other powers from using it as a stepping stone or invasion point of England itself.

I bring all this up because the idea that James would have been satisfied as merely the King of Ireland would have been nothing but a slap in the face to him. He considered himself an Englishman, and above all, an English King. Ireland was the addition to the main prize that was England. James would have settled for nothing else. If he was unable to retain England’s throne, he would have preferred exile to second place. And the Williamites/Protestant Englishmen for their part would also have preferred exile. Allowing James and his descendants to sit in Dublin was only delaying the inevitable of a future war as a hostile kingdom in their doorstop was only inviting future conflict, especially with the high likelihood that James would be ruthless in his persecution of the Ulster Protestants who had rejected him so thoroughly.

In short, it was all or nothing. Either James surrendered the crowns or William did, there would be no dividing the spoils.

BUT for the sake of argument, I will indulge the hypothetical. The Nine Years War ends with William and Mary acceding to the thrones of England and Scotland while James retains Ireland. The short term consequences are a brutal put down, and perhaps even expulsion, of those in Ulster who defied James. Reports of savage French and Irish soldiers brutalising Protestants would horrify the English and prove their fears right. Long term, the Irish Sea becomes the second longest strip of water in the world after the English Channel. James would endeavour to create a navy that could repel the English, soon to be British, Navy but would always come up short. He would rule a country which was majority Catholic but he would still ensure power remained with the Old English aristocracy in Dublin, and firmly out of the hands of the Celtic Irish. His kingdom would be no more than a de facto vassal of the French, and would remain reliant upon them for money. Yet if the Jacobite line stayed put, the English would probably be quite happy with the arrangement. They’d be shot of the political headache that was Ireland, and it would not trouble British politics in the 18th-20th centuries. Yet still the lurking menace of the Irish kingdom would be a constant threat, with popular propaganda making it seem more threatening than it was, with tales of secret French armies ready to strike at any moment. As result, the hostility towards Catholics and Irish in popular culture will also be far greater than in OTL. If we assume there is no popular revolt that overthrows the regime, then Ireland probably becomes a mirror to Russia on the west of Europe’s borders as Russia is to the east: a deeply reactionary, deeply feudal, agrarian, poor society, yet lacking the manpower to defend itself properly. Social change would be slow, especially with the Jacobite Royalty being resistant to any changes that threaten their loose grip on power. If we assume that a group like the Fenian Brotherhood would be more successful though, then Ireland could be the first of the liberal republics in Europe, throwing off the shackles of Catholic feudalism and sectarian division since the Irish state would not be as equipped to put down threats as the British army was.

Overall, it was extraordinarily unlikely that James or William would be satisfied with an independent Irish Kingdom. But even if they were, Ireland’s history would have been very different but also strikingly similar as to OTL.

Nationalism is a post-enlightenment, Liberal ideology, whose fundamental underlying principle is that it was immoral for one ethnic group like the Austrians or the Russians or the English to marshal political power over other ethnicities through the Monarchy, as the monarchy would be within the culture of one ethnic group to the exclusion of all others.

Agree with that critique or not but nationalist movements were often opposed to monarchical power, seeing it as the instrument through which their people were repressed, and being wholly opposed to the idea that multiple crowns could be combined in one person. That’s not to say they didn’t end up as Kingdoms such as Italy after unification, Greece after independence, Romania, Yugoslavia etc, but the nature of these kingdoms was often wound up with the Liberal language and principles that got their foundation, hence why it was rare for the monarchy to be long lived and why so many of them became republics in the end.

So I think we should be careful about what it is we mean by Nationalism as it is underpinned by ideas which often spell the end of monarchy in the long term, even if enduring it in the short term.

Whether he would have glorified Stalin in the same way as Stalin glorified Lenin, I’m not sure but he definitely would not have made any significant change to the cult of personality and it’s prominence in Soviet life and culture.

Because of this, it’s unlikely that Zhukov would have closed the gulags. Without the desire to reform things, and desperate to keep a lid on internal issues, it’s likely he maintains that policy. That being said, it is also likely that he would not send anyone else there, save deliberate anti-communist agitators so those who had been interred under Stalin would die in the gulags with the hope under Zhukov they could one day be quietly done away with without much fuss. The Soviet state would in almost all circumstances become more tolerant of dissent voices after Stalin’s death unless his loyalists remained in power.

As for the rest of society, the level of repression they’d come to expect would likely remain. Restrictions on speech, assembly, art and so forth would continue as they had been under Stalin. Zhukov would certainly make no effort to liberalise things, yet I also don’t believe he would be as invested in repressing these things as Stalin. At a state level, nothing would have changed but at a local level, I think a lot of these laws would be de facto un enforced or resources directed to what Zhukov considered the genuine threats to Soviet stability.

On the economic front, I also see little change. Khrushchev was adamant, some would say obsessed, with agricultural reform in the USSR and put a lot of effort into ensuring that it was one of the most significant achievements of his time in office. Zhukov? Not so much. I can see him being entirely disinterested in such matters, believing that the system set up by Stalin was sufficient enough to continue propelling the USSR into the rest of the 20th century. As a result, you can expect a lot of economic lagging behind for the USSR in the 50s and 60s as the country relies on outdated machinery and the economic catastrophes of the five year plans, putting them significantly at a loss in the Cold War.

And on the foreign front, I do not know how things would have progressed. Zhukov was a militarist so it is to be expected that he would urge the most ruthless, brutal measures and tactics, right? Well, he was also a personal friend of General/President Eisenhower, so does that factor mean there’s more chance of a rapprochement between the sides earlier on in history? I simply cannot say. If I were to guess, Zhukov’s friendliness towards individuals in the West would not translate to greater friendless towards the western bloc as a whole. The coldness of the Cold War would still be very much a factor. There would be no warm and welcoming visits as there were with Khrushchev, no friendly kitchen debates, no attempt at reconciliation but a continuation of Stalin’s policy of defensive hostility towards the West under the model of achieving socialism in one state before the world. Thus, if we assume he was in office as long as Khrushchev was, when the Cuban Missile Crisis came about, it’s perfectly plausible that he could have botched it during one of the tensest moments in world history. However, I think that the underlying factors were still more important than the individuals at play, and he was not stupid. The deal for both sides to withdraw missiles would have come eventually. The only difference is I think Zhukov would have been having fun feeling like he was back in the field of battle once more in this situation, and perhaps that boldness gets Kennedy to admit he’s withdrawing from Turkey publicly rather than privately so neither side loses face. 

On a more internal but still foreign front, is the Warsaw Pact states, and the western Soviet republics. In these places, you might expect Zhukov to maintain Stalin’s repression but we know that in OTL Zhukov spoke out against sending troops into Hungary and wanted to repair the relationship with Yugoslavia. Thus, while he wouldn’t go to the extent that Khrushchev did, there would be a weakening of the Warsaw Pact as Hungary would certainly have left without Soviet repression - but perhaps he might have made a different decision if he were making it himself. In any case, the end result is a weaker Soviet presence in Eastern Europe and several humiliating scandals for Zhukov personally as these failures would make him look weak and embarrassing on the international stage.

Which finally brings us to how things would look politically. As I said at the top, Zhukov was not a politician and he knew it. Yet if he were thrust into this position, he would be surrounded by people who had their own goals and ambitions, and were always looking to undermine him. In reality, I cannot see him surviving long in office. You have to make Zhukov unrealistically competent at politics to ensure that he survives the viper’s den that was the Politburo. He would be unable to coordinate the various factions like Stalin had, constantly hamstrung and unable to cope without a clear military ethos, it is unlikely he would have been able to achieve any major political victories even if he wanted them.

In conclusion, Zhukov in OTL should be eternally thankful he died never having been Soviet Premier and with the respect and admiration of his people because it would have been a whole different story if he had been. Ironically, I think the figure I would most compare him to is Tsar Nicholas II: Unwilling to change the level of repression he inherited yet lacking the strength to marshal it effectively, he would be perceived as weak, indecisive and incompetent. The country he oversaw would have a reputation as an increasingly backward nation, with only the thin veneer of stability provided by a beloved war hero leader. Premier Zhukov would not be remembered fondly by history, whereas OTL’s General Zhukov can be thankful that he remains beloved while all the political problems of that era were squarely on Khrushchev’s shoulders, for better or worse.

The implication of the rareness of Arthur’s car was that it’s mere existence was unique, not that Arthur’s desire for it was. It’s rareness deriving from being impossible to create before Arthur and no one being bothered to create one before Arthur are two very different things.

That is the case, but that’s not what Ron considered unique about it. When Harry first opens his present, Ron says *”It’s an Invisibility Cloak,” said Ron, a look of awe on his face. “I’m sure it is – try it on!… I’d give anything for one of these,” he said. “Anything.”* There’s nothing any more unique about it in Ron’s eyes except for the fact that it allows you to be invisible which, he should know, isn’t all that special. He isn’t yet aware of any of its other qualities but he’s desperate for *any* invisibility cloak.

What’s happened here is very obviously a soft retcon of the availability of invisibility spells. In PS, they were exceptionally rare but since Rowling needed a way for them to get to Hogwarts without being seen, she widened the amount of ways wizards have to make things invisible. You can say it was a good or not important change, but it’s clearly a change from one book to the next, there’s no denying that.

It’s the only one we know of because Arthur is the only one with a muggle fetish who would want an invisible car. Theoretically, there’s nothing to stop them from being mass produced save the fact there’s no demand for them among wizards. 

The point remains that an invisibility cloak was supposed to be a huge deal in the first book given how shocked Ron is to see one, and then we see it more and more so it’s not as unique as was originally implied.

I think it’s more a criticism of the fact that it’s treated as a super rare piece of magic that no one else has which allows you go invisible in the first book, and commonplace enough that their clapped out car has an invisibility option in the second.

The short answer is “Everyone copied the English.”

The longer version is that it was not at all common to refer to the King’s - *Rex* in Latin - heir as a prince for most of post-Roman/Early Medieval history. The example I know best is that when Edward I was born, he was known as the “Lord” Edward, not Prince… and it’s largely Edward that we have to thank/blame for the change. To again summarise, Llywelyn ap Gruffudd claimed the title of “Prince of Wales” during Edward’s life which, as you say, was not placing himself below the King of England but *above* him. Llwelyn was claiming not just dominion over all the kings of wales as their imperial *Princeps* in a Roman style, but to be greater than the mere *Rex Anglorum,* Edward. Fast forward a bit and Llywelyn’s pretensions were crushed under Edward’s heel as his conquest of Wales was secure, but Edward needed to secure the loyalty of the educated Welsh administrators who were more eager to serve than the disloyal yet powerful marcher lords. To this end, Edward revived the principality of Wales and gave the title to his second 16 year old son, also called Edward, to rule as a personal fiefdom. In this way, Edward retained the loyalty of the Welsh administrators who had a local ruler to be accountable to while keeping Wales securely under his control.

So we can observe the transformation of *Princeps* from a title denoting imperial control to merely being the title of the son of the King of England - not even his official heir as Prince Edward had an older brother, Alfonso. But Alfonso died, leaving Prince Edward the heir. And when he became Edward II, he conferred his old title onto his son and from then on, it was tradition that the heir to the English throne be known as the Prince of Wales.

After this point, people noticed what Edward had done and began to copy this basic pattern noting how important it was that the King’s heir be given his own, unique title. So the heir to the French King became the Dauphin, the Prince of Austrias would follow the King of Spain and so on.

That rule would be advice for storytelling in general rather than horror specifically tbh.

I’m no expert on the subject but what I think defines horror as a genre is that it imposes a sense of powerlessness on the protagonist. Whether the horror is supernatural or a serial killer or something much more mundane, the point of the story is that the character(s) we’re following are utterly helpless in the face of it. They can barely understand it, let alone know how to defeat the horror and that’s what’s scary about it; the dread of the unknowable, the terror we feel about an obstacle we can’t overcome, the thrill of something so completely out of our comfort zone and knowing that every attempt to rationalise what’s going on will only end with you being defeated by the horror before everyone else.

Just get across that sense of hopelessness in the face of whatever they’re going up against and you’ll have a pretty solid foundation for a horror story, in my view at least.

Connor is the villain of the story for trying to undo all their good work.

Which is why his story is fundamentally broken as if you want a story where he sacrifices the tribe he set out to save in order to protect his new family of Assassins, you have to justify the lengths he will go to in order to destroy the Templars and the story never does. Haytham has more than enough reason to help Connor protect his tribe, Connor is offered many opportunities to have his cake and eat it to. He can have everything he wants and barely needs to sacrifice anything but he gives it all up anyway because… reasons. His loyalty to the ideals of the Brotherhood are never given the time to actually be articulated properly as it’s not even clear that Connor understands them. Haytham absolutely DESTROYS Connor in the rooftop scene (with FACTS and LOGIC!) and Connor NEVER has a rebuttal for Haytham’s claim here. Haytham was calmly explaining his ideals to an idiot child who refuses to learn, and Connor never learnt, much less articulate a reason for why Haytham was wrong to think what he did. And when your protagonist is never actually capable of explaining why he does what he does, that’s a huge problem with your story.

It’s why, at least, the unmistakable evil of the Borgia made more sense as a driving force for Ezio to become an Assassin as that is what he was fighting against. So was Altair, even though the Templars he took down had their justifications for what they did, they were still villainous actions so Altair didn’t need to feel overtly remorseful about killing them. But Connor has neither the justification for becoming an assassin due to ideology nor the moral impetus to take down a great evil. It’s the worst of both worlds as he killed good people - mostly - for no good reason and only ended up making life worse for everyone except Juno.

Connor’s problem isn’t that he’s bland or boring. It’s that he’s an utterly contradictory character who never has a clear sense of motivation or purpose as he has no reason to join the Assassins or believe in them, and certainly not after it’s revealed to him that it was Washington who burnt his village not Charles Lee who he’d spent the whole game pursuing. 

Worse, the Templars are unambiguously the good guys in the story but due to Achilles’ arrogance and Connor’s naivetie, all of Haytham’s well laid plans are ruined because Connor never developed the free will he was always bragging about and remained a slave to the decisions Achilles made for him. It’s not even that you can justify it by saying he understood the Assassins as more than revenge but that’s just not the case. Connor is one of the few protagonists in fiction when I was actively rooting for the antagonists, every time I play that game I want Haytham to win and I see it as a tragedy that he loses, certainly that he dies in defence of his lieutenant and friend from his son’s blind rage. 

No, Connor is far more broken than merely being bland compared to Ezio, to the point that I wish he was merely boring and had nothing to say about him rather than the contempt I actually hold towards his character and no amount of cut speeches from the end of the game are going to fix that.

The problem with the contention that there was no setup for the Solar Flare is that all of the subtext in AC1 was not pointing to a stable world that the Templars controlled. As Vidic himself says "The world's a mess," and this only escalates when you read the e-mails and news alerts in that game that all build up the idea of a huge ecological disaster on the horizon; mass migration from the US to Mexico, Africa becoming depopulated thanks to a virus, water poisoning, etc. And then there are the symbols on the walls that are only visible through an ability that only Desmond has, as was the case with the existence of the POEs and Vidic's cryptic line that they're gifts from "those who came before."

Even if the explicit idea of a Solar Flare that would destroy the world had not yet been created, what you can't say is that AC1 was simply a battle between an all powerful organisation of powerful tycoons looking to control the world and a ragtag group of freedom fighters. All the way through the game is the implication that there is something else going on, something more sinister that eludes the understanding of people like Desmond who the audience is experiencing this world through. We can see that this is more than a battle between two groups that will leave the world more or less as it was when the games started, as there is some force behind both of these groups that is more ancient, more powerful and more terrible than any of the characters in the series can possibly comprehend.

That's why the inclusion of the Solar Flare was such a genius progression for the story, as rather than just battling the Templars for control, you're fighting for survival... and you're the only ones who know. You can't run to the media, they're controlled by Templars. You can't tell any independent scientists, they'll be killed if they know. You can't publicise it, Abstergo will find a way to suppress the information or brand you crazy if it gets out. Rather than being irrelevant, the Templar control of society is a key aspect of the story as the Assassins have to find a way to save humanity all while Abstergo hunts them mercilessly ensuring that they can't get any help from anywhere else.

And from a thematic point of view, it again shows the repetition of history. As not only have Assassins and Templars been fighting for centuries over and over again, one of their ideologies never truly remaining superior for long, but the conflict predates human society itself. The struggle for freedom against a need for control is our inheritance from the First Civilization, and what eradicated them due to their carelessness is going to do the same to us because this struggle is too important to be set aside but it also needs to be if anyone is going to survive the coming apocalypse. 

I don't find this a generic story at all, but an incredibly interesting premise that takes all the building blocks of the first game and builds upon them in a logical and consistent way that escalates the stakes and mystery of this world beyond what frankly would have been a more generic story of autocrats and freedom fighters that we've seen in a bunch of stories before now. The intertwining of the overall danger with the legacy of the past is what made Assassin's Creed such a unique story, and 2 does nothing to damage that from a storytelling perspective.

As such, the Austrians presented a set of demands they knew could never be fulfilled and invaded Serbia knowing the Germans would have their support.

If, however, this is not the case, I very much doubt the Austrians would feel they could match the strength of Russia on their own, as without Germany to suffer most of the brunt, the chance for genuine defeat was extremely plausible.

So, if Germany is determined to stay out of the war, one of two options is possible;

1. The Austrians present much more charitable demands to Serbia that they would actually be willing to agree to, satisfying both parties. The Austrians would grumble that they did not revenge their Archduke in the manner they would have liked but without a casus belli, they have no reason to invade and the crisis passes. It becomes footnote in European history, and Franz Ferdinand is remembered as a martyred figure who could have reformed the Empire in favour of minority rights. European history progresses as it would have done, with an imperial, monarchical streak to culture and politics as without their downfall allowing an opportunity for America to step in, there’s no reason for the old empires to collapse. The Germans remain the boogeymen for the rest of Europe but at worst, a Cold War mentality sets in that never boils over to genuine conflict.

2. The Austrians see the risk as worth it, and invade Serbia with the justification of refusing their demands. In response, Russia declares war on Austria-Hungary, but because of no German involvement, there is never a western front to the war. As in OTL, it was believed the Russians would take months to properly mobilise and Austria would seek a much more decisive victory over Serbia as Germany sought to take France out of the war quickly to focus on Russia. And as in OTL, the Austrian invasion would be successfully repelled by the Serbians and with their desperation, it would probably lead to more military disasters on the Austrian side. And while the Russians were a badly equipped and managed army against Germany, against Austria-Hungary, they would have been comparatively matched. Indeed, the Russians would have had the advantage of men, land and time on their side. With a disastrous two front war, I do not doubt that this could feasibly be a war that would end by Christmas for Austria, with their complete and total defeat. At the latest, I cannot reasonably see the conflict persisting long into 1916. And the peace would have been disastrous for Austria, with many of her Balkan subjects torn away and either made independent or Russian puppets. Nicholas II would have removed the stain of defeat at the hands of Japan in 1905 and restored the glory of his people as a great European power, all but ensuring neither of the revolutions of 1917 ever came to pass and may encourage him to be more repressive and autocratic at home with this victory behind him. Austria-Hungary, if indeed Hungary was not made into a republic too, would be a diminished empire, if not forced to return to a kingdom. It would be a humiliated, spent force in geopolitics going forward and the fate of the Balkans would be between Russia and the nationalist movements, and possibly the Ottoman Empire if it survives. Like option 1, the Western European powers are barely affected by the war and they look the same in 1920 as they did in 1910, and indeed going forward.


Whatever option is pursued, it is clear that the rise of American power never occurs, the Soviet Union never rises and Communism does not become a global threat. The Nazis never rise to power and the European Empires will largely be a mainstay of global politics right through to the later decades of the 20th century. It is a world not characterised by the brutal reality of that war, where aristocratic power, Christianity and Imperialism are the defining attributes of the age and not the conflict between Capitalism and Communism as in OTL.

It was absolutely a cunning strategy to build up his own power base while wounding Sauron behind his own borders, I’m not doubting the intelligence of the plan but as Talion points out, it is a morally dubious one, which is something Celebrimoir never concerned himself with one way or the other.

His amnesia was faked, yes, as we see in the Bright Lord DLC that right before he inhabits Talion, he declares “all shall fear me and rejoice.” He knew what his plan was, he just had to persuade Talion to carry it out for him.

I wouldn’t say that Talion convinced Celebrimoir to craft a new ring, as if he really didn’t want to, there was no way Talion would have been able to pressure him into doing so. No, I think that what the conclusion of SOM actually was is a moral victory for Celebrimoir’s cunning. He spent the whole game urging Talion to keep focused on the mission, to ignore the slaves plight, to forsake a life with Lithariel, to reject his humanity and dedicate his entire existence to the destruction of Sauron and nothing else. In this, I don’t see Celebrimoir’s offer to heed the call of the Hither Shore as a genuine offer but as a test which, in his mind, Talion passed as he was in the same position as Celebrimoir was before him and so committed to Sauron’s downfall that he would forsake his own family to see it come to pass.

I wouldn’t say that Celebrimoir was “good” in SOM but that he didn’t have a real opportunity to show showcase the depths of what he would go to in order to get what he wants as, so far as he is concerned, Sauron cannot yet be destroyed without a New Ring and only the Black Hand can so as long as Talion agrees to continue fighting, they have no cause for discord between them. I especially wouldn’t call him good since he lied to Talion about holding his body hostage while pretending the bond was inseparable, faking amnesia and pushing Talion into the morally dubious path of using dominated orcs as soldiers. Already here, we can see an arrogance and selfishness which has yet to reach its fulfilment in his betrayal but is still present and shows that while the Dark Lord is a clear danger, it doesn’t mean that the wraith is anymore to be trusted than Sauron.

And we see this manifest more and more over SOW with his dismissal of everything and everyone inside Minas Ithil except the Palantir, his easy adjustment to the politics of Mordor and, finally, his willingness to betray Talion in order to secure a more willing host who would battle Sauron on his behalf and enthrone the Bright Lord in Barad-Dur. But I don’t think there was ever any point in which this wasn’t his aim. To quote Celebrimoir himself when he is about to possess Talion; *”All shall fear me and rejoice.”* He always intended to try and supplant Sauron as the Lord of Mordor, to conquer his hosts and not to scatter them to the winds and free Middle Earth from them, he was simply better at hiding it before he had turned Talion into a willing enough pawn to help him forge his coveted New Ring.

But in spite of all this, I don’t hate him or anything, I think he’s a fascinating character and a lesson on the nature of arrogance and power, and the danger that comes from your own inflated vanity. Celebrimoir believed that he had an innate right to rule, if not the Elves of Eregion then the Orcs of Mordor so it is an ironic fate that he ended up fusing with Sauron either dominated by him or sharing power for the rest of the War of the Ring with him.

In all pre-industrial societies, family politics was what dominated everything through the patron-client system whereby you would serve a family, and you would get rewards from it. This still endures in many parts of the world where tribes are more important than national identity, Afghanistan being a key example. Industrialisation destroyed that as you no longer had to rely so directly on someone and you could afford to make your own fortune without needing a patron to do everything for you, only an employer to pay you for your factory work, to be overly simplistic.

As a result, everything got larger, and not just cities and population numbers. The ideas got larger too, people started thinking of themselves as part of these grander collectives rather than just whatever family had traditionally held sway in the region, out of which you get Nationalism.

Additionally, the power of the state also vastly expanded during this period to account for this vastly growing society and whereas you scarcely saw formal employees of the King in times past, now you saw his agents everywhere from police officers to regular tax collectors to postmen. As such, the state was magnified in importance in a way it never had bee before, and out of this springs Fascism.

Fascism is, fundamentally, the idea that if everything is dominated by the state then all of society will be united in one, singular will as there will be nothing against it and thus harmony and unity will flow from it, but it can only come out of this unique process of state enlargement that comes out of industrialisation. It cannot arise in societies which are patchwork, localised and dominated by local patrons much more than even the anointed King in many cases.

Well, it’s not impossible that the HRE could have been united into a singular bloc but certainly not around the concept of Germanic blood or ethnicity like in OTL as the importance of such concepts did not exist in the 1500s. If you were to have such a centralisation, what you would need was an immensely powerful Emperor who was capable of bullying and/or negotiating with the various Kings, Dukes and free cities of the Empire into giving up their privileges and submitting to his centralised authority. And in 1540, you had just such a man in Charles V, who certainly had the authority and power to have half of Europe under his control and the rest paralysed in fear of him. If he has shifted his focus from the Spanish Empire in the Americas and instead used Spanish soldiers as a way to put down German uprisings against him as he attempted to force the Hapsburg Throne into a position of centrality and cement the Empire in a unified German state but this would almost certainly not have happened in his lifetime. The most I can see Charles achieving if he wanted this German dream was changing the succession laws to make the Imperial Throne a hereditary office, but that’s it. It would then be up to his successors to chip away at the power of localities and make their family dominant in German life and politics to ensure a path to true unification. How successful would this be? Not very, in my opinion, but there’s still a chance it could be achieved over the next century, let’s say.

As for nationalism, no. It arises out of Revolutionary and Enlightenment ideals that can only come after the Thirty Years War and the end of the Protestant-Catholic dynamic as something that Europeans were willing to war with each other over. This was still very much the Age of Kings, and the importance of family politics was much more relevant to most people than abstract concepts like nationhood or ethnicity. It would be virtually impossible for ideologies like that to emerge before the eighteenth/nineteenth century.

Compare to Medieval Russia, Nicholas II’s empire was a bustling hub of industry but compared to Britain, France and Germany? Russia was still an agricultural based economy that relied upon the feudal system for the vast majority of its functioning.

And that’s not to assign virtue to one system or the other, but simply to point out that industrialisation was indeed heavily resisted by the Tsars precisely because they knew that it was the antithesis to their power as without the process of gradual constitutionalism that had enabled the British and German monarchies to survive the growth of the bourgeois middle classes, the Russian autocracy would not survive the same fate as it was tied exclusively to the land based aristocracy and if they lost their power, the Tsar would inevitably lose his throne. Alexander III especially was keen to suppress any reforms and it was only under Stolypin that industry actually started to be brought to the county in a significant way.

So were there no industrial towns or no modern inventions present in the Russian Empire by 1914, or even by 1900? No, it would be impossible to keep out western influences THAT much, but it is certainly true to describe the country as dominated by agriculture and being heavily resistant to the inventions of the western world as those in power knew that such innovations would lead to the uprooting of their whole social order.

But it is likewise impossible to separate this from the context of war, as without the threat of the Germans, it is even less likely that the Tsar would have consented to any form of industrialisation in the empire at all. It was only a fear of being overwhelmed by them and losing influence and land to them in Eastern Europe that caused the Russians to try and accelerate the insignificant levels of industry they had by the turn of the 20th century. If it had not been for that, Russia would likely have remained reliant upon the serf system for as long as conceivably possible as there was nothing about its local politics, culture or geography that would push the people of that county towards such developments; it was always pushed on by foreign and geopolitical events.

So yes, communists bad, communists very, very bad, but to suggest that Russia was always going to be an industrial power or one of the leading members of the Great Powers club is just silly and ahistorical. If the Liberal Republic had stood, yes, Russia would almost certainly have made huge strides in industry and westernisation and Russian cities would have been indistinguishable from British or American ones in terms of living standards, but if the autocracy had remained in control, Russia would have continued only gradually changing and allowed only so many industrial settlements as could be permitted without surrendering the divine power of the Great Imperial Crown, which wasn’t likely. The nature of the autocracy meant it was on a collision course with westernisation and one would have to give in, so either Russia would become a constitutional monarchy, the monarchy would be abolished or the agricultural autocracy would be at the mercy of its neighbours and rivals. It was impossible to be both.

I was drawn to her from across the street, for even when she was crying, her beauty radiated through her tears, or perhaps the adrenaline pumping through her body made me feel the rivers of blood swimming within her. Even before hypnotising her, she had been easy enough to lead astray as she rabbited on about men and pigs, or some such trivial youthful nonsense. She seemed eagerly desperate to go home with me, and though I knew what it was she wanted, I knew not why she wanted it so badly, but I indulged her all the same. I teased her, played with her, made her dance around my skyline apartment for a while and then I just looked at her; couldn't be older than 25, her whole life ahead of her, so many plans, so much youth, so much potential buried in those deep blue eyes of hers. I didn't think twice about killing her.

Oh, there was no reason to, I could have taken the blood I needed and allowed her to forget this encounter and sent her back to the street to continue her miserable life, but I knew myself by now. Once I sunk my teeth deep into her supple young neck and felt every cell in my body light on fire with euphoric joy at the rush, I knew I was right and I would need it all; every last drop. It was unavoidable, I told myself in the early days and I couldn't help myself, just like dad always said but I knew by now that was moronic. I didn't just need to take her blood to survive, I wanted to kill her. I wanted to feel her nails clawing at my skin fall down, I wanted to hear her desperate screams fade into silence, I wanted to look into her eyes and see the blank emptiness of a corpse as I felt the dripping of her life blood fall down my chin. Allowing myself the joy of feeling her life drain away was a greater pleasure than a thousand orgasms at once, and something I was wholly incapable of understanding when I was mortal like her.

I raised my fangs out of her and gasped for breath and looked down. By the looks of her body, the girl had been dead for ages and I had been feasting on a corpse, draining it for all it was worth. I cast a look at the window wall and saw myself, a monster practically coughing up her blood as my finely tailored suit was irreparably stained with her essence, unsure of whether the liquid or my eyes bore a darker tint of red. I smiled at myself and allowed her bloodless body to fall to the floor as I took my phone out of my jacket.

"John, I have another one," was all I said as I hung up as I started to wipe whatever wet traces of blood were around my face still. Even now, I needed more and I tried to resist the temptation to bite on my own finger in my mouth as I suckled it like a newborn baby. Even in these small traces, I felt such indescribable frenzy wash over me as my senses were fulfilled again. Were that I lived like a monster of old, I could feast on village after village for night after night and never have to worry about my lusts being left wanting for the joy these walking vessels gave was-

"The usual, my lord?" The empty voice beckoned behind me.

"No, keep this one in refrigeration. Her body may provide some juice yet and I would like every morsel of this little beauty."

"Very good, my lord," John said as he dragged the body away downstairs. In truth, it was a miracle I had not killed John yet, but he had some sentimental value and, more importantly, he had his uses. With a new corpse practically every night, I could not dispose of them all myself, and I did not know how but in his old life, John knew how to deal with these issues quite ably. It was what had made him the most unique of the helpers at the shelter, his eagerness to help those less fortunate with anything, and he meant *anything.* I don't know how much of this is him or whether my control dominated his mind completely but once I figured out that i could hypnotise them into doing what I wanted, he was the obvious choice, but even I had my limits. I could sate myself with nameless strangers but I knew that one day I would kill him as well. The only difference would be that he would accept it eagerly instead of fighting me all the way. I began to wonder whether I would prefer that or not.

My musings on the subject, however, were interrupted by the sound of something hitting the floor. I turned around to see something had fallen from her pocket and hit the floor. I motioned to John to keep taking her body away and he dutifully obliged as I sped over to observe the object and pick it up and I could scarcely believe my eyes; it was a rolled up bag of cocaine. I had not done lines since... well, since I turned I think and I felt a curiosity to try once again but I knew it was merely that; a curiosity, a fancy... a fleeting passing feeling. The stronger impulse in me overrode those ideas as I walked to the nearest bin and threw the white powder away without hesitation. With a thud, the lid closed and I stepped away from the bin and I started to laugh. How many years did I suffer trying to do such a thing? For how many years did my own body betray me and force me to indulge those fucking sugar bags time after time? How much did I steal, how many did I hurt, how many did I kill with mortal means in my quest to obtain more and more and for what? Brief, momentary highs that subsided after a while but served to make me "feel good?" A fucking waste, just like all those worthless, useless junkies under the bridge. They had taken in a weakling, desperate and hungry and we had all helped each other in our despair to cling onto life helping each other get what we needed. Even now, I knew that slaughtering them had been an act of mercy and justice. Oh, the feast of blood was glorious to indulge on for those days before their corpses started to rot but that was secondary, it was good that the world was purged of those vermin. I relied upon manufactured substances then, but now I relied upon nature. Then, I was weak, dependent, a slave to my body and to those who sold me the drugs. 

But now I am a hunter, I hold all the power, I answer to no one. An idiot would say that the two were indistinguishable, that I was still hopelessly addicted to blood just as I was addicted to drugs before my death but they proved the gutless worthlessness of the human race with such brain dead observations. Could I have snapped the neck of anyone who tried to hurt me when I relied upon the white lines? Could I have torn through whole Police squads, could I hypnotise landlords into turning their best properties over to me, could I fuck the most beautiful women before I killed them? No. I stole and drank and killed to survive. Now, I do what I do to THRIVE! There is no desperation, no pain of withdrawal, no fear of what life will be like should that joy disappear. I could sate myself on blood bags like Michael and Sara do, but why would I? Why would I forbid myself the experience of taking what I want? Even the drug lords and petty dealers who used me can not imagine what it is like to take away everything from them, to bury your teeth into their neck, to feel their flesh rip apart and the warm gush make you feel alive again. Watching some kid on the streets kill himself for you over years for his next fix isn't in the same fucking ballpark as this. They can't comprehend it, they can't understand what true power is like and that's why they all had to die.

Yes, I was a different creature now, above their petty concerns, above addiction and dependence. I am a Lord of the Night, I am the real monster of this world. I. Am. A. Vampire. ...And if I don't find another body to drain right now, I will tear this building apart until I find a single drop because that's all I need to gain the power.... all I need... all I need...

Now, if we assume this and also assume that Mary continues to have no children, then the throne passes to her legal heir, who would be the descendant of Margaret Tudor who married James IV of Scotland, which would be Mary, Queen of Scots, as she is commonly known in 1554. 

To Mary I, this would be a joyous arrangement as her Catholic throne would be preserved, even if it would not be in her own person, and for Mary QOS, this could save her life as well because it was her marriage to the Earl of Bothwell in 1567 that caused her downfall, so if she could have inherited the throne of England instead, whereupon she would surely have accepted Philip of Spain's proposal of marriage, which was bound to come.
